rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / DICTIONARIES AND TUPLES / CHAPTER 9

slides.title: Dictionaries
slides.main: A dictionary looks up by a meaningful key, not by number — and does it instantly.

items.title: Gently
items.sub: A default value instead of an error

body.text: Phone by name, price by title, setting by word — that's how we look things up in life.

slides.title: Creating a dictionary
slides.sub: Pairs separated by commas, key and value by a colon
slides.main: Keys are unique, values are anything: numbers, strings, lists, even dicts.

body.text: ON SCREEN
{'apple': 50, 'banana': 70}

slides.title: Access by key
slides.sub: The key goes in square brackets, not a number
slides.main: The key must exist: otherwise Python stops with a key error.

body.text: ON SCREEN

50
KeyError: 'kiwi'
The code reads itself: prices["apple"], not prices[0].

slides.title: The get method
slides.sub: Polite access: no error, a fallback value
slides.main: Brackets when the key must exist. get when a missing key is normal.

cells.title: d[key]
cells.sub: No key — error: a loud bug

slides.title: Add and change
slides.main: No key — a pair is added; key exists — value replaced. Insertion order is kept.

body.text:
prices = {"apple": 50, "banana": 70}
prices["kiwi"] = 90      # new pair
prices["apple"] = 55    # replacement
print(prices)
ON SCREEN
{'apple': 55, 'banana': 70, 'kiwi': 90}
No indexes: not "what is third" but "what lies under this name".

slides.title: Key check: in
slides.sub: The word in looks at keys, not values
slides.main: Key lookup is instant — ten pairs or ten million.

body.text:
prices = {"apple": 50, "banana": 70}
print("apple" in prices)       # True
print(50 in prices)             # False — that's a value
print(50 in prices.values())    # True
Why so fast — covered in the algorithms course: hash tables.

slides.title: Deletion
slides.sub: del and pop go by key, len counts pairs
slides.main: A list's remove searches by value; a dict does everything by key.

body.text:
prices = {"apple": 50, "banana": 70, "kiwi": 90}
del prices["kiwi"]
print(prices.pop("banana"))   # 70
print(prices, len(prices))
ON SCREEN
pop(key, 0) won't fail on a missing key; clear() empties everything.

slides.title: Looping over a dict
slides.main: The best way is items(): two names in the loop header, the pair unpacks itself.

body.text: ON SCREEN

apple 50
banana 70

slides.title: Counting frequencies
slides.main: The pattern "get with zero plus one" replaces a separate counter per word.

body.text: First "yes": get returned 0, we added 1. Second: took 1, added 1 more.

slides.title: What keys can be
slides.main: Keys compare exactly: "Apple" and "apple" are two different pairs.

slides.title: References and copies
slides.sub: The same rules as for lists
slides.main: b = a — one name for two; a real copy is .copy() or dict(a), and it is shallow.

body.text:
a = {"x": 1}
b = a             # the same dict
c = a.copy()      # a real copy
b["x"] = 99
print(a, c)
ON SCREEN

slides.title: Typical mistakes
slides.sub: A key not found, and size change in a loop
slides.main: Reading an unreliable key — use get. Looping over a dict — don't change its size.

body.text: Also: in looks at keys; case and spaces matter; a dict has no indexes.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: A dict is "key — value" pairs: read, change and delete by key.

items.title: Dictionary
items.sub: Curly braces; keys are unique and immutable

items.title: Keys
items.sub: in checks keys, del and pop remove a pair
